q: Inky, firmly tannic, and yet almost every sparkling Shiraz leaves the cellar with a generous dosage. What is the sugar doing in a wine like that?
opts: Covering under-ripeness, the style being built on fruit picked early and green for acidity
Cushioning the tannin, which carbon dioxide sharpens beyond what a still red would show
Raising the pressure, since a sweeter dosage means a livelier mousse
Deepening the colour, pigment binding to sugar as the bottle ages
exp: Carbonic acid and the scrub of the bubbles both amplify bitterness and astringency, so tannin that reads supple in a still Shiraz turns aggressive under gas, and the dosage is a counterweight rather than a sweet tooth. The serious versions are traditional method from fully ripe, often old-vine fruit with years on lees, and the sugar is calibrated against the tannin exactly as it is against acidity in colder places.

q: The first bottle-fermented sparkling wine South Africa ever put on sale was made in 1971 under an Afrikaans name, and the label is still poured today. Give that name.
exp: Frans Malan of Simonsig made it from Chenin Blanc in 1971 and sold it from 1973 once its lees ageing was done, years before the Cape had a category to put it in; the phrase means Cape sparkle. The wine later moved over to the Champagne varieties, and when the industry needed its own term for the method two decades on, this bottle stood as the precedent: claim the method, name the Cape.

q: A Pipers River label begun in the mid-1980s as a Champagne house's Tasmanian joint venture takes its name from the patronymic of Abel Tasman himself. Name the label.
exp: The partner was Louis Roederer, whose venture with Heemskerk was the first serious Champagne investment in Tasmania and settled the question of whether the island could carry the traditional method. The label later passed to the Hill-Smith family and marketed its wine as Methode Tasmanoise, a joke with a point in it: name the place, borrow nothing.

q: For the better part of a century Australia's festive sparkling red sold under a borrowed French name, retired once place-name protection reached the shelves. What was the style called?
exp: The style dates to the 1890s at Great Western in Victoria, where a Champagne-trained cellar hand put the local red through a second fermentation, and burgundy in that era was British shorthand for any soft red rather than a claim about Pinot Noir. Agreements with Europe struck the borrowed names off Australian labels, so the wine was rebadged sparkling Shiraz, which had been the grape inside all along.

q: On the Carneros highway stands a copy of an eighteenth-century Champagne residence, built as the public face of one house's American venture. Which house?
opts: Taittinger
Louis Roederer
Moet et Chandon
Piper-Heidsieck
exp: Domaine Carneros, opened at the end of the 1980s, is modelled on the Chateau de la Marquetterie, the Taittinger property near Epernay, and the theatre is deliberate: a visible chateau announces a long commitment in a landscape of sheds. Moet had led the way into California in 1973 with Domaine Chandon at Yountville but kept the architecture Californian, and Piper-Heidsieck's venture ran under the Piper Sonoma name.

q: Korbel prints California Champagne on its labels to this day, and no American regulator objects. What protects the wording?
opts: A licence from the Champagne trade body, renewed by a royalty on every bottle sold
American law treats champagne as a common noun that any producer remains free to adopt for a sparkling wine
A grandfather clause: labels approved before the 2006 accord with Europe keep semi-generic names beside their origin
The wine is traditional method, and in American usage the word certifies method rather than place
exp: The 2006 agreement froze the semi-generic names rather than abolishing them: no new label may take up champagne, chablis or burgundy, while brands already holding approval carry on, provided the true origin stands beside the borrowed word. That is why the survivors are old California brands, why the class shrinks by attrition, and why no new producer can ever join it.

q: A grower family from Bethon in Champagne planted Chardonnay and Pinot Noir at thirteen hundred metres in the high desert of an unlikely American state. Which state?
exp: Gilbert Gruet planted near Truth or Consequences in 1984, on cheap land whose altitude does what latitude will not: desert nights cold enough to hold acidity through a fierce summer. The family's Albuquerque winery built its reputation on traditional-method Brut priced against far grander addresses, and the lesson travels: a sparkling base is a question of site arithmetic, not postcode.

q: Its Champagne parent transplanted the house rules to Anderson Valley whole: every grape from its own ranches, and reserve wines raised in oak for the blend. Name the California estate.
exp: Roederer arrived in 1982, chose fog-cooled Anderson Valley over the safer prestige of Napa, and refused bought fruit from the first vintage. The oak-aged reserve wines are the signature it shares with the parent house, and the vintage prestige bottling, L'Ermitage, made the case that American traditional method could age. The operation reads less like a subsidiary than a second house.

q: Same Canelli grower, same Moscato Bianco: one bottle wears a wire cage and reaches about seven percent alcohol, the other a plain straight cork, a soft prickle and five. Which is which?
opts: The caged bottle is Asti, the corked one Moscato d'Asti
Both are Moscato d'Asti, bottled at the two pressures the rules allow
The caged bottle is Moscato d'Asti, the corked one Asti
The caged bottle is Brachetto d'Acqui, the corked one Moscato d'Asti
exp: The two share a denomination and a grape; the fork is how far the single fermentation is allowed to run. Asti ferments on to full spumante pressure and a couple of points more alcohol, so the closure must be the caged mushroom cork, while Moscato d'Asti is arrested sooner, keeping more sugar and staying below the sparkling threshold, which is why it may seal and pour like a still wine.

q: Dry Lambrusco and sweet Asti both take their sparkle in tank, yet only one of them ever gets a second fermentation. Which one, and why?
opts: Both referment; sparkle made in tank is a second fermentation by definition
Neither referments; tank sparkle is dissolved into the wine under pressure rather than fermented
The Asti: reaching full pressure on grape sugar alone takes a second fermentation on top of the first
The Lambrusco: a finished dry base wine referments in tank, where Asti is one fermentation stopped partway
exp: Asti's tank run starts from must and simply never finishes, which is where its sweetness and low alcohol come from; there is nothing left over for a second act. Lambrusco is made as an ordinary dry wine first and then set going again in tank with a measured addition, which is why it can finish bone dry at normal strength. One name covers two genuinely different sequences, and each wine has the one it needs.

q: One member of the Lambrusco family covers more Emilian vineyard than any other. Name it.
exp: The name records its tight, cylindrical bunches, shaped like little salami, which in Emilia counts as affectionate. It anchors the workhorse blends around Reggio and Modena and holds a denomination of its own at Santa Croce, and blenders lean on it for colour and easy fruit rather than for structure.

q: Ripeness shows in one Lambrusco's very name: as harvest nears, its stalks and bunch stems flush red. Name it.
exp: Graspa is the local word for the stalk, and the red flush runs through stem and leaf as the fruit comes in. It grows on the foothills south of Modena around Castelvetro and gives the fullest and grippiest wine of the family, the one traditionally poured against the fattest plates on the Emilian table.

q: A tall swan neck with a bulge at its base sends much of the rising vapour back down into the pot before it ever reaches the condenser. What does that do to the spirit?
opts: Lightens it, because heavy compounds fall back
Raises its congener load, because the vapour condenses twice over
Darkens it, because copper is stripped from the neck into the vapour
Lowers its strength, because alcohol condenses before water does
exp: The effect is called reflux: the heavier compounds condense early, drop back into the pot and are distilled all over again, so the spirit that reaches the condenser is the lighter fraction. It is why a tall narrow still gives a more delicate spirit than a short fat one of the same capacity. Contact with copper rises along with it, which strips sulphur compounds out of the vapour as a bonus.

q: Two linked columns, an analyser fed with wash and a rectifier that returns its condensate to be stripped again, let one apparatus run without ever being emptied. Whose patent of 1830 was that?
opts: Robert Stein
Aeneas Coffey
Edouard Adam
Eugene Charmat
exp: Coffey's design is the ancestor of every continuous still working today, and grain whisky, most vodka and most rum all pass through one. Stein's earlier continuous still was superseded within a couple of years, Adam is remembered for condensing apparatus, and Charmat's name belongs to sparkling wine rather than to spirits.

q: Neither the first nor the last part of a pot still run is thrown away; what is held back goes into the charge for the following run. What is that returned material called?
exp: They are rich in the heavy oily compounds the stillman rejected, and redistilling them recovers the alcohol without letting those compounds into the hearts. A still house wastes very little: even the spent wash goes to cattle feed.

q: European law stops calling a distillate a spirit drink of its raw material, and calls it ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin instead, once it passes a fixed strength. What strength is that?
exp: Above that point the distillate has lost the fingerprint of whatever it was made from, which is why vodka can come from grain, potato or grape and taste of none of them. Whisky rules run the other way and cap distillation below 94.8 percent so the cereal survives into the glass.
